summary: Diazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine used for the management of anxiety disorders and short-term relief of anxiety symptoms, symptomatic relief of acute alcohol withdrawal, adjunctive relief of skeletal muscle spasm, and adjunctively in convulsive disorders. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance and is habit forming, with a boxed warning for risks of concomitant opioid use, abuse/misuse/addiction, and dependence/withdrawal. It has a long half-life and an active metabolite (desmethyldiazepam, half-life up to 100 hours). Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration and taper to discontinue; abrupt withdrawal can be life-threatening (seizures).
indications: Management of anxiety disorders or short-term relief of symptoms of anxiety
Symptomatic relief of acute alcohol withdrawal (agitation, tremor, impending/acute delirium tremens, hallucinosis)
Adjunct for relief of skeletal muscle spasm (reflex spasm, spasticity from upper motor neuron disorders, athetosis, stiff-man syndrome)
Adjunct in convulsive disorders (not effective as sole therapy)

moa: Diazepam is a benzodiazepine that produces anxiolytic, sedative, muscle-relaxant, anticonvulsant, and amnestic effects. Most effects are thought to result from facilitation of the action of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, by binding the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor.

preg: Benzodiazepines cross the placenta. Use late in pregnancy can cause neonatal sedation (respiratory depression, lethargy, hypotonia) and/or neonatal withdrawal (hyperreflexia, irritability, restlessness, tremors, inconsolable crying, feeding difficulties); monitor exposed neonates and manage accordingly. Published observational data do not report a clear association with major birth defects. High single doses during labor/delivery may cause fetal heart rate irregularities, hypotonia, poor sucking, hypothermia, and moderate respiratory depression. Avoid unless clearly needed. A National Pregnancy Registry for Psychiatric Medications exists (1-866-961-2388).
lact: Diazepam is present in breast milk (about one tenth of maternal plasma concentrations). Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions including sedation and withdrawal in breastfed infants, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with diazepam.
hepatic: Contraindicated in severe hepatic insufficiency. In mild and moderate cirrhosis the average half-life is increased (reported 2-fold to 5-fold, with individual half-lives over 500 hours), volume of distribution increases, and clearance decreases by almost half; half-life is also prolonged with hepatic fibrosis (mean ~90 hours) and hepatitis. Reduce dose and titrate cautiously in hepatic impairment.

major: Opioids - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death; reserve for patients without alternatives, limit dose/duration, and monitor closely

Other CNS depressants (phenothiazines, antipsychotics, anxiolytics/sedatives, hypnotics, anticonvulsants, narcotics, barbiturates, anesthetics, sedating antihistamines, MAO inhibitors, antidepressants) - potentiated CNS depression
Alcohol - additive CNS depression, may be fatal
moderate: CYP3A4/2C19 inhibitors (cimetidine, ketoconazole, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, omeprazole) - increased and prolonged sedation
Phenytoin - metabolic elimination of phenytoin may be decreased by diazepam
minor: Antacids - ~30% lower peak diazepam concentrations and slower absorption, without change in extent of absorption
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; a moderate fat meal delays and decreases absorption (Cmax ~20% lower, AUC ~27% lower).
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; concomitant use enhances the sedative effect and combined CNS depression may be fatal.
interactions.diagnostics: Periodic blood counts and liver function tests advisable during long-term therapy (isolated reports of neutropenia and jaundice); minor EEG changes (low-voltage fast activity) of no known significance may occur.

counsel: This medicine is habit forming; take exactly as prescribed and do not increase the dose on your own
Do not use with opioids or alcohol unless directed - risk of severe sedation and death
Do not stop suddenly; the dose must be tapered to avoid withdrawal, which can include seizures
May impair driving and operating machinery; avoid until you know how it affects you
Store securely to prevent misuse or diversion
Tell your clinician if pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding
Report excessive drowsiness, trouble breathing, yellowing of skin/eyes, or unusual mood/behavior changes immediately
pk: Rapid; >90% absorbed orally, distribution half-life ~1 hour
Peak plasma concentration in 1 to 1.5 hours (range 0.25 to 2.5 hours)
Terminal elimination up to 48 hours; active metabolite desmethyldiazepam up to ~100 hours
Store per product labeling at controlled room temperature
pearls: Schedule IV controlled substance and habit forming; dependence and withdrawal increase with higher dose and longer duration
Long-acting with an active metabolite (desmethyldiazepam, half-life up to ~100 hours) - effects and accumulation persist
Abrupt discontinuation can cause life-threatening withdrawal (seizures, delirium tremens); always taper with a patient-specific plan
Contraindicated in severe respiratory insufficiency, severe hepatic insufficiency, sleep apnea, myasthenia gravis, and acute narrow-angle glaucoma
Metabolized by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19; inhibitors (cimetidine, fluoxetine, omeprazole, ketoconazole, fluvoxamine) prolong sedation
Flumazenil reverses sedation but can precipitate withdrawal/seizures and is contraindicated when given for a life-threatening condition such as status epilepticus
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next scheduled dose, in which case skip it and resume the regular schedule. Do not double up. Because diazepam is habit forming, do not change the dosing schedule without medical advice.
overdose: Overdose causes CNS depression ranging from drowsiness, confusion, dysarthria, lethargy, diminished reflexes, ataxia, and hypotonia to respiratory depression and coma; rarely paradoxical disinhibition. Combination with other CNS depressants, alcohol, or opioids may be fatal. Markedly abnormal vital signs suggest co-ingestants. Manage with general supportive measures including IV fluids and airway management. Flumazenil may reverse sedation but can precipitate withdrawal/seizures (especially with chronic use, dependence, or co-ingestion of seizure-threshold-lowering drugs) and is contraindicated when a benzodiazepine was given for a life-threatening condition such as status epilepticus. Contact Poison Help (1-800-222-1222).
